newsitem.title: GERMANY: German insurance buyers bemaon lack of rating data.
newsitem.headline: German insurance buyers bemaon lack of rating data.

text.p: German industry is benefitting from falling prices in industrial insurance, but is unhappy about the growing non-transparency of pricing mechanisms.

"Insurers will eventually be forcing their customers to put all insurance out to tender," Guenter Schlicht, managing director of the German risk managers' association Deutscher Versicherungs-Schutzverband (DVS), said at DVS' general meeting on Friday.
Bonn-based DVS represents 4,000 companies, municipalities and utilities in insurance matters.
"In industrial fire, premium income fell in 1996 by 4.5 percent to four billion marks," said Schlicht. But in the same year insurers still recorded a market profit of 50 million marks.
The new in-house tariffs drawn up by Allianz, Gerling and Colonia contained many elements DVS had long advocated, such as a more precise recognition of an individual company's risk situation.

"However, we have problems with the transparency or rather the non-transparency of the pricing mechanism," Schlicht added. In-house tariffs were closely guarded secrets. But if insurers kept their benchmarks in the risk assessment process to themselves, the basis for the desired dialogue with their customers was very thin.
Schlicht was critical of "high premium levels" in environmental liability insurance. Insurers' complaints about underwriting losses were difficult to comprehend, as they presented "no solid figures".
"German industry is not prepared to fund, with today's high premiums in environmental liability, the losses of yesteryear or the day after tomorrow," Schlicht said.
He was in favour of Germany removing any special exemptions for insurers from anti-cartel rules. The upcoming amendment to the German anti-trust law should be used for that purpose.
Schlicht added that the high German premium tax of 15 percent may, in an open European market, cost German insurers a lot of business.

He also warned that current trends in motor insurance were not always comprehensible and might undermine the solvency of some companies. Ratings would thus in future be all the more important in the German market.
